The purpose of operating a business is to make money.

I'm not arguing that they "aren't allowed to generate a profit anymore" but merely pointing out that if you're generating profit it is by definition always for a specific thing or entity, and this thing is always to serve the interests of the customers that this business represents. Either internally via equity or employment or externally via product. Not just generating profit for the sake of generating profit - which, if this was the case - would be the business equivalent of a Rube Goldberg machine. And that this profit might not necessarily be monetary I.E., a charity - despite what you think of it - can still be classed as being a successful business if it meets the function it was set out to do towards it's customer base.

You don't seem understand the concept of equity or have any semblance of how corporations - as it extends to publicly traded companies with limit liability and CEOs elected from the shareholder body, anyway - are run. As I have previously stated investors and employees are customers of a business as equally as consumers are, For example you could have the most solvent bank in the world but if the majority of clientele of that bank lose confidence in how that bank is run then they'll simply withdraw their funds from the institution leaving things to go tits up - or get bailed out by the government as the case is nowadays. In fact the largest most power corporation to ever exist was simply dissolved via an act of parliament where upon it was nationalized as part of the British government.

Profitability is important in that it determines how attractive as an investment product a company is - if publicly traded anyway - in terms of how much stock value it's able to hold or how much of a dividend it's able to pay. Or how easily it is to capitialise projects in leverage I.E., borrow money. But even then this simply comes back to how it's able to serve the interests of it's customers I.E., shareholders or creditors. On the other side of the coin - and a counter point to your argument - employees may actually have no interest in how profitable a company is - and whether they get tasked with cleaning empty buildings - as long as they get paid, for example if you're a programmer at a major publisher it's practically a given that you're going to be given the boot after the project is completed no matter how profitable it is, so in that context you have to ask yourself why you would continue to work at the joint when you could possibly just go into a startup where you would at least have some share in the equity rather than just getting a - ridiculously large, admittedly - salary. Which represents a huge opportunity costs to said employees. It is by no accident that businesses tend to spend massive amounts on pampering their employees with shuttlecock machines - for example. In fact in making that point you've defeated you're own argument because if money was the end goal of everything people would be perfectly willing - if paid enough - to clean empty buildings because that would be their sole care.

Anyway - to get back on point - your reasoning isn't making much sense here: Saying the goal of a business is to be more profitable is like saying that the purpose of efficiency is to be more efficient. That is you've confused the function of a thing to it's form. Rather the goal of a business is to serve the interests of it's customers in the most efficient I.E., making the most money by spending the least, I.E, Profitable, way possible. A "tunnel rat" infantryman is lowered into an enemy Viet Cong tunnel complex by members of his reconnaissance platoon. Viet Nam. 1967

During the Vietnam War "tunnel rat" became a more or less official specialty for volunteer infantrymen, primarily from the United States and of small stature, who would be sent in to explore and sabotage the extensive Viet Cong system of tunnel complexes. They had built underground hospitals, training grounds, storage facilities, headquarters and more. The Viet Cong might stay underground for several months at a time and the tunnels were their territory so it was an incredibly dangerous job.

Whenever troops would uncover a tunnel, tunnel rats were sent in to kill any hiding enemy soldiers and to plant explosives to destroy the tunnels. A tunnel rat was equipped with only a standard issue .45 caliber pistol, a bayonet and a flashlight, although most tunnel rats were allowed to choose another pistol with which to arm themselves. The tunnels were very dangerous, with numerous booby traps and enemies lying in wait.
